text_blocks.snippet: High blood pressure (hypertension) is diagnosed when your blood pressure readings are consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg.
Blood pressure is recorded as two numbers:

list.snippet: Systolic (top number): The pressure when your heart beats.
Diastolic (lower number): The pressure when your heart rests between beats.

text_blocks.snippet: According to the American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, blood pressure categories for adults are defined as follows:

snippet_links.text: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

list.snippet: Normal: Less than 120 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic.
Elevated: 120–129 mm Hg systolic and less than 80 mm Hg diastolic.
Stage 1 Hypertension: 130–139 mm Hg systolic or 80–89 mm Hg diastolic.
Stage 2 Hypertension: 140 mm Hg or higher systolic or 90 mm Hg or higher diastolic.
Hypertensive Crisis (Emergency): Higher than 180 mm Hg systolic and/or higher than 120 mm Hg diastolic.

text_blocks.snippet: You only need one of the numbers (systolic or diastolic) to be in a higher range to be classified at that level. A single high reading does not mean you have high blood pressure. Doctors look for consistent high readings over time before making a diagnosis.

If your reading exceeds 180/120 mm Hg, wait one minute and test again. If it remains this high and you experience symptoms like chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness, or changes in vision, call 911 immediately.
